lines.say: In 1950, a baby born in Spain could expect to live about 62 years. A baby born in Norway, almost 72.
Today, Spain is one of the longest-living countries in the world, at almost 84. And it's ahead of Norway.
This is how southern Europe overtook the north, and what happened in the east along the way.

card: Life expectancy at birth: how long a baby would live if that year's death rates never changed
lines.say: First, what the number means. Life expectancy at birth is how long a baby born in a given year would live, if the death rates of that year stayed the same all its life.

card: It shows how healthy a country is in that year. Deaths in childhood pull the average down a long way
lines.say: So it isn't a forecast for anyone. It's a snapshot of how healthy a country is in that year. And when many babies die young, the average falls a long way, which is why the early figures are so low.

card: Each square is one country: the brighter, the longer people live. Source: UN, via Our World in Data
lines.say: The figures come from the United Nations' World Population Prospects, through Our World in Data. Each square on this map is one country, and the brighter it is, the longer people live.
1950. Europe as a whole: 62 years, well above the world average of 46. At the top: Norway at 71.6, the Netherlands at 71.4 and Sweden at 71.1, all in the north-west.
Further south and east, the numbers are much lower. Italy, 65.7. Spain, 61.8. Portugal, 58.5. Albania, 44.5.

lines.note: 1950 · 27 years between the top and the bottom
lines.say: Between the top and the bottom of this map, that's a gap of 27 years.

lines.note: Died before age 5, 1950 · Portugal 15% · Spain 10% · Norway 3%
lines.say: Much of that gap is children. In 1950, about one child in ten in Spain died before turning five. In Portugal, about one in seven. In Norway, one in thirty.
Then comes the long climb. Through the 1950s, 60s and 70s, almost every country adds years, and fast.

card: Far fewer deaths in childhood, vaccines and antibiotics, clean water and better food
lines.say: Far fewer children die young. Vaccines and antibiotics reach almost everyone. Clean water and better food do the rest. In Spain today, about one child in 300 dies before turning five.
By 1975, Europe's average has reached almost 71, nearly as high as Norway's was in 1950.
Spain is climbing fastest of all. It has already passed Germany and the UK.
And in 1982, Spain passes Norway. Since 1950, it has added about five and a half months of life expectancy every single year.

lines.note: 1990 · Europe 73.1 · gap top to bottom: 9.8 years
lines.say: By 1990, Europe's average is 73, and the gap between the top and the bottom of the map has shrunk to about ten years. Portugal, the lowest in western Europe in 1950, has gained almost 16 years.
But watch the east. As the Soviet Union breaks up, life expectancy in Russia falls, from 69.3 in 1990 to 63.8 in 1994.
The Baltic states fall too. Latvia drops from 69.5 in 1990 to 65.2 in 1994.
By 2000, Russia is still only at 65. Ukraine, Belarus and Moldova are lower than in 1990 too. Researchers link it to economic collapse, alcohol and strained health systems.

lines.note: Spain vs Russia · 7.7 years apart in 1990 · 14.4 in 2000
lines.say: For a decade, the gap between east and west grows instead of shrinking. Spain and Russia were 7.7 years apart in 1990. By 2000, 14.4.
Meanwhile, the south keeps on climbing.
By 2019, the top three on our map are Switzerland at 83.8, Spain at 83.5 and Italy at 83.3. Spain started ten years behind Norway. Now it's ahead.
Italy did the same, passing Norway in the late 1980s. In 2019, Switzerland is the only country on the map ahead of both of them.

lines.note: Portugal passes Germany in 2010 and the UK in 2014
lines.say: Portugal, which started at 58.5, passed Germany in 2010 and the UK in 2014.
Then comes the pandemic. Here are the last few years, close up.
Europe's average falls from 78.8 in 2019 to 77.0 in 2021, the biggest fall since these figures begin, in 1950.
Some countries lose much more. Bulgaria drops by 3.7 years, and Russia by 3.3.
Others barely notice it. Norway's figure doesn't fall at all, which is why Norway was briefly back ahead of Spain, from 2020 to 2022.
Then it recovers. By 2023, Europe is back to 79.1, higher than before the pandemic.
2023. Switzerland, 84.0. Italy and Spain, 83.7. Then France, Norway, Malta and Sweden, all about 83.3.
Further down: Germany at 81.4 and the UK at 81.3. Both are now behind Spain, Italy and France, and behind Portugal and Greece too.

lines.note: Lowest on the map · Ukraine 73.4 · Russia 73.2 · Moldova 71.2
lines.say: Then Poland, 78.6. Hungary, 77.0. Romania, 75.9. Bulgaria, 75.6. And lowest on the map: Ukraine at 73.4, Russia at 73.2 and Moldova at 71.2. For comparison, the world average is 73.2, the same as Russia's.

Since 1950, Spain has gained almost 22 years, and Portugal almost 24. The biggest gain on the map is Albania's: 35 years. Albania, at the very bottom in 1950, now lives longer than Poland, Hungary or Croatia.

card: Lower heart disease, diet, family ties into old age, health systems that reach almost everyone. No single answer
lines.say: Why the south? Researchers point to several things, and no single one explains it: lower rates of heart disease, diet, strong family ties into old age, and health systems that reach almost everyone.

And Germany is the puzzle. It spends about 8,300 dollars a year per person on health, adjusted for prices. Spain spends about 4,900. Yet a baby born in Spain can expect to live more than two years longer.
Three things to take away. One: Europe as a whole gained 17 years of life expectancy, from 62 in 1950 to 79 in 2023.

take: Spain and Italy now outlive Norway, Sweden and Germany
lines.say: Two: the south overtook the north. Spain and Italy now live longer than Norway, Sweden and Germany.

take: The east fell behind, then climbed back
Russia lost more than five years in the early 1990s
lines.say: Three: the east fell behind in the 1990s, Russia by more than five years, and it is still catching up.
Next on Terrachart: who works the longest hours in Europe. It's not who you think.
Sources are in the description. Why do you think Spain and Italy live longer than Germany and the UK? Tell us in the comments.
